content: 1. Cheng et al. (2012) in Tanzania identified factors contributing to potential misdiagnosis in HIV testing. Similarly, Boeras et al. (2011) in Lusaka, Zambia, and Rwanda, as well as Granade et al. (2004) in the USA, reported on diagnostic challenges. Kanal et al. (2005) in Cambodia and Learmonth et al. (2008) across 26 countries also highlighted issues in diagnostic accuracy. Sacks et al. (2012) in the UK and Wolpaw et al. (2010) in South Africa further emphasized the importance of addressing diagnostic errors. 2. Adebayo et al. (2012) in Nigeria and Mashauri et al. reported that 7% of individuals (534/7,007) could not be conclusively diagnosed. A follow-up study revealed that 43% (346/8,017) of individuals previously diagnosed as HIV-positive could not be conclusively confirmed. At the time of these studies, many sites initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) did not routinely implement retesting. 3. Results from external quality assessment (EQA) schemes, also known as proficiency testing, were reported in three studies. These studies compared laboratory results to assigned reference values. In 2006 and 2011, concordance rates ranged from 88% to 90%. However, declines in concordance were noted in 2008 and 2010, attributed to health worker shortages caused by natural disasters. 4. Two studies from Ethiopia demonstrated good performance in proficiency testing schemes, with overall agreement rates between 95% and 100%. Errors leading to incorrect results included the use of a tiebreaker strategy, difficulties in interpreting weakly reactive test lines, and stock-outs of reagents. 5. Clerical errors were reported in 14 studies. These errors, while not always leading to misdiagnosis, included poor record-keeping, data reporting issues, labeling and transcription mistakes, and specimen mix-ups. One study found that poor record-keeping resulted in nearly 30% of errors leading to incorrect test statuses. 6. User errors were identified as a potential cause of misdiagnosis in 21 studies. These errors included incorrect specimen collection, misinterpretation of results, and reliance on a single assay testing strategy to issue an HIV-positive diagnosis. Some providers over-interpreted faint test lines, leading to incorrect HIV-positive diagnoses. 7. A study involving specimens from 26 countries used photographs of test lines from rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) to assess laboratory technicians' proficiency in reading and interpreting results. Specimens with very weak dilutions of HIV-1/2 antibodies were less accurately reported. Similarly, a study from Uganda found that most false-reactive test results were associated with weak test lines on RDTs. 8. A UK study assessing visual interpretation of false-reactive and true-positive readings reported that most false-reactive specimens had fainter test lines compared to true-positive specimens. Both studies speculated that faint test lines contributed to the misdiagnosis of HIV infections. 9. Poor management and supervision practices were reported in 20 studies. These included the use of damaged or expired test kits, stock-outs, incorrect RDTs for HIV testing, and failure to use timers or correct reagents. One study from Tanzania found that a syphilis RDT was being incorrectly used to test for HIV infection. 10. Errors related to poor management and supervision also included testing clients during the window period, under-trained or ineligible staff performing HIV testing, and low levels of retesting before ART initiation. High workloads and stress were linked to user and clerical errors in several studies. 11. The use of a tiebreaker testing strategy was associated with substantial levels of false-positive test results and potential misdiagnoses. For example, in Brazil, a tiebreaker was used three times, two of which led to false-positive results. Studies from Uganda reported false-positive rates of 437% and 482% when using a tiebreaker strategy. 12. Cross-reactivity and individual characteristics were reported as potential issues in nine studies. These included biological interactions due to antibodies from concurrent infections, adverse environmental exposure to assay components, HIV subtype variations, and interactions between test kits in an algorithm. 13. Poor management of supplies, user errors in interpreting weak reactive test results, and the use of a tiebreaker strategy were identified as key factors contributing to misdiagnosis. To ensure accurate results, all staff providing HIV testing must be adequately trained and certified. 14. Training, including pre-service, in-service, and periodic refresher training, is essential to maintain and improve the quality of services. Participation in proficiency testing schemes allows sites to monitor performance, identify issues, and address challenges such as interpreting faint lines and addressing health worker shortages. 15. User errors in interpreting faint lines and weak reactive test results were a common challenge, often leading to substantial levels of false-positive results. This issue has been well-documented in the literature, but challenges with over-interpretation persist. 16. Addressing this issue may require specialized training for health workers and collaboration with manufacturers to improve instructions for interpreting faint lines. Standard operating procedures at the site level should guide health workers on handling faint lines when they occur. 17. No assay or testing algorithm is perfect, and false-positive and false-negative test results should be anticipated. However, this review highlights errors and practices that compromise the reliability of test results, particularly the use of a tiebreaker testing strategy. 18. The review suggests that the tiebreaker strategy increases the likelihood of false-positive test results and potential misdiagnosis. National programs and policymakers must select and use appropriate testing strategies and validated algorithms. 19. The World Health Organization (WHO) has never recommended the use of a tiebreaker testing strategy, yet it appears to be common practice in many settings. WHO recommendations emphasize retesting individuals diagnosed as HIV-positive before they enroll in care and/or treatment. 20. This review suffers from publication bias, as it focused on identifying studies related to the misdiagnosis of HIV status in published and gray literature. Limited data on the magnitude of misdiagnosis within HIV testing programs make it difficult to determine whether misdiagnosis is negligible or simply not monitored. 21. The consequences of misdiagnosis are serious at both individual and public health levels. Ensuring the quality of HIV testing services and accurate HIV diagnoses is an urgent priority. Quality management systems must be implemented to minimize the risk of incorrect test results.
